answers.gloss: A TE node is a traffic-engineering abstraction of a node within one specific layer network, rather than the physical device across all layers.
answers.example: ROADM R1 represented as a node in the OTN layer topology.
answers.relations: It is part of i.tetopo; i.telink objects run between TE nodes; i.tp, i.ttp, and i.tcep objects may be located on it.

answers.gloss: A termination point is owned by or located on a TE node and is the point where a TE link terminates. In this model it is specifically a link-facing termination, not a generic service endpoint or an internal tunnel-connection endpoint.
answers.example: tp-R1-R2 on R1 terminates the R1-R2 TE link at R1.
answers.relations: It is on i.tenode and terminates i.telink. It may participate in the cross-layer support represented by i.stp, but it is distinct from tunnel head i.ttp and internal tunnel endpoint i.tcep.

answers.gloss: A supporting TP denotes the cross-layer supporting relationship by which a client-layer TP is supported by a server-layer TP. Despite its label, the modeled concept is the adaptation/support relationship, not merely another standalone point.
answers.example: An OTN TP at R1 supported by an optical-layer TP at R1.
answers.relations: It relates TPs across client and server layers and supports i.tp; it captures layer adaptation rather than adjacency between nodes.

answers.gloss: A tunnel termination point is the trail head at which a TE tunnel originates or terminates on a node.
answers.example: ttp-A1 at A1 is the originating head of the A1-A3 ODU2 tunnel.
answers.relations: It is on i.tenode and originates or terminates i.tunnel. Unlike i.tp it is not defined as a TE-link termination; unlike i.tcep it is the tunnel's trail head rather than an endpoint of an internal tunnel connection within an intermediate or tunnel-participating node.

answers.gloss: A TE tunnel is an end-to-end engineered tunnel through a TE topology that realizes a service. It is the engineered connectivity construct itself; the model does not separately represent an external service contract.
answers.example: The A1-to-A3 ODU2 tunnel engineered over the OTN layer network.
answers.relations: It runs from and to i.ttp objects, is engineered over i.tetopo, has node-local connection endpoints represented by i.tcep, and may be labeled with i.otnlabel.

answers.gloss: An OTN label encodes the tributary-slot and tributary-port-number multiplexing resources used for OTN carriage, such as the slot structure for mapping an ODU into a higher-rate container. It identifies allocatable multiplexing resources as part of expressing that adaptation.
answers.example: The TS/TPN values selecting the tributary slots that carry an ODU2 in an OTU4.
answers.relations: It labels i.tunnel with its OTN multiplexing allocation; its semantics concern OTN slot/resource selection and mapping structure.

answers.gloss: A connectivity matrix expresses which internal connections are permitted within one TE node, constraining switching among the node's termination-side resources.
answers.example: R2's matrix permits connection from one ingress TP to a selected egress TP but forbids another pairing.
answers.relations: It is scoped to i.tenode and constrains internal connectivity among termination points or their associated switching resources; it does not describe inter-node links.

answers.gloss: A TE link is a traffic-engineering adjacency between TE nodes within one layer network.
answers.example: telink-R1-R2 connects R1 and R2 in the OTN topology.
answers.relations: It is between i.tenode endpoints, is terminated by an i.tp at each end, and is contained in i.tetopo.

answers.gloss: A TE topology is one per-layer traffic-engineering network. In this model a single topology object does not itself denote an undifferentiated multilayer domain; different layer networks are related through support/adaptation.
answers.example: The OTN layer network containing its OTN TE nodes and TE links.
answers.relations: It contains i.tenode and i.telink objects; i.tunnel is engineered over it. Cross-layer support is represented through i.stp rather than by treating this topology as inherently multilayer.

answers.gloss: A tunnel connection endpoint is a node-local endpoint of a connection belonging to a tunnel, including at nodes participating in the tunnel's realization.
answers.example: tcep-a1a3-R1 is the connection endpoint for the A1-A3 tunnel on R1.
answers.relations: It is on i.tenode and part of i.tunnel. It is distinct from i.ttp, which is the end-to-end tunnel trail head, and from i.tp, which terminates a TE link; this model does not assert that those objects are identical even if implementations associate them.

answers.gloss: A node is a forwarding-node abstraction in the single unified multi-layer topology. It is not defined as a separate per-layer copy of a physical device, although a physical device such as R1 may supply its identity.
answers.example: ROADM R1 represented once as a forwarding node in the OTN-over-optical domain.
answers.relations: It is part of t.topo. Topological t.link objects run between nodes; t.ltp, t.sip, and t.cep objects are located on nodes; t.translink and t.nrg are scoped at a node.

answers.gloss: A link-termination-point is a node-owned edge point at which a topological link terminates. It is link-facing and is distinct from external service access and connection endpoints.
answers.example: nep-R1-R2 on R1, where the R1-R2 link terminates.
answers.relations: It is on t.node and terminates t.link. It is distinct from t.sip, which exposes service access, and t.cep, which is an endpoint of a service connection.

answers.gloss: A transitional link represents same-node adaptation between layer structures, not inter-node adjacency. Its client/server sides express a mapping such as a lower-rate client signal into a server container; the model records it as a link-like adaptation construct rather than merely another termination point.
answers.example: The OTU4/ODU2 adaptation at R1, mapping an ODU2 client structure into an OTU4 server structure.
answers.relations: It is at t.node and adapts the layer or multiplexing structure expressed by t.lpq. Its endpoint classes and direction are not separately formalized beyond the client/server adaptation semantics.

answers.gloss: A service-interface-point is the node-local hand-off through which an external client accesses a connectivity service.
answers.example: sip-A1-odu, the ODU2 client hand-off at A1.
answers.relations: It is on t.node and accesses t.cs. Unlike t.ltp it does not terminate a topological link; unlike t.cep it is the external service-facing access point rather than an endpoint of the internal connection realizing the service.

answers.gloss: A connectivity-service is the externally consumed end-to-end connectivity service, not a separately modeled engineered tunnel or path.
answers.example: cs-a1a3-odu2, the ODU2 service offered from A1 to A3.
answers.relations: It uses t.sip access points, is realized by t.cep connection endpoints, is qualified by t.lpq, and runs over t.topo. The model has no separate tunnel object representing its engineered path.

answers.gloss: A layer-protocol-qualifier expresses the protocol/container and multiplexing relationship of a signal, such as an ODU2 mapped into an OTU4 server. It does not identify a particular allocation of tributary slots or a tributary-port number.
answers.example: The qualifier 'ODU2 mapped into OTU4' on the A1-A3 service.
answers.relations: It qualifies t.cs and is the layer/multiplexing structure adapted by t.translink.

answers.gloss: A node-rule-group defines node-scoped constraints on which ports or termination-side resources may be internally cross-connected.
answers.example: R2's rule group permits selected ingress-to-egress cross-connects and prohibits other port pairings.
answers.relations: It is on t.node and constrains internal switching connectivity, rather than inter-node t.link adjacency.

answers.gloss: A link is a topological adjacency between two forwarding nodes in the unified multi-layer topology. It is not defined as belonging to a separate per-layer topology object.
answers.example: link-R1-R2 between forwarding nodes R1 and R2.
answers.relations: It is between t.node objects, terminated by t.ltp objects, and contained in t.topo. Same-node cross-layer adaptation is represented separately by t.translink.

answers.gloss: A topology is the single multi-layer topology describing the whole domain, rather than one topology object per layer.
answers.example: The unified OTN-over-optical domain containing its forwarding nodes and links.
answers.relations: It contains t.node and t.link objects and is the topology over which t.cs is provided. Layer adaptation within the domain is represented by t.translink at nodes.

answers.gloss: A connection-end-point is a node-local endpoint of a connection that realizes a connectivity service.
answers.example: cep-a1a3-R1, the R1 connection endpoint for the A1-A3 service.
answers.relations: It is on t.node and part of or realizes t.cs. It is distinct from external t.sip access and link-facing t.ltp termination; the model does not assert that those points are identical.

proposals.rationale: Both denote a node-owned, link-facing edge point at which a topological/TE link terminates, and both explicitly exclude service and internal connection endpoints.

Despite different labels and link-versus-support framing, both modeled concepts denote the same-node cross-layer client/server adaptation relationship rather than inter-node adjacency or a standalone point.
Both are node-scoped switching constraints specifying which termination-side resources may be internally connected, and neither represents inter-node connectivity.
